title: Open model admission and profiling pipeline: automated intake, conversion, validation, and catalog publish
creator: Aisha Kapoor
description:
Goal: build a fully automated, auditable pipeline to admit open-source LLM checkpoints into Redwood's model catalog and publish verified performance profiles. The pipeline covers: 1) secure intake of upstream weights (HF urls, s3 manifests), 2) deterministic hashing and provenance recording, 3) conversion to the runtime optimized artifact format, 4) functional and regression validation (generation, streaming, KV cache correctness), 5) performance profiling under representative workloads (latency P50/P95, throughput under standard batching, memory footprints), and 6) publish to model-catalog with version pins, quantization recommendations, and rollback metadata.

Scope: implement end-to-end automation for the common case (PyTorch HF-style checkpoints + transformers config). Exclude exotic model families (mixture-of-experts, non-transformer architectures) for this iteration. Deliverables: orchestration pipeline (Airflow/Argo job definitions), conversion container (model-converter v2), a standardized verification test-suite, perf harness config, and a catalog publishing job that emits a signed performance profile JSON and creates the model entry in the catalog UI.

Acceptance criteria:
- New model intake triggered via a manifest URL completes successfully in CI within a reproducible environment and records provenance (source URL, commit/sha, HF model_id) in artifact metadata.
- Converted artifact runs end-to-end on the runtime image without OOMs on the baseline test instance and passes the functional test-suite.
- Performance profile contains P50/P95 generation latency for three sequence-length buckets, throughput at batch sizes [1,4,16], and peak GPU memory.
- Model entry created in catalog with version pin and recommended quantization profile; release engineers can opt-in to canary rollout.
- Security review checklist completed for weight provenance and KMS usage.

Notes on design decisions and trade-offs:
- Deterministic hashing: we will prefer SHA256 over ad-hoc fingerprinting. We will store provenance in S3 alongside artifacts and in the catalog DB.
- Conversion path: prefer a single canonical conversion container that produces both an fp16 and an int8-friendly artifact. Avoid creating many intermediate formats to reduce drift between conversion and runtime.
- Perf profiles: to keep CI time reasonable, use representative micro-benchmarks plus a longer nightly job for full sweep across batch sizes and seq lengths.

Risks:
- Some community weights expect nonstandard loading code (missing config or custom layers); these will land in a manual triage queue rather than blocking the automated happy path.
- Quantization regressions: recommend conservative int8 suggestions initially and mark as experimental until further evals.
